question.leadin: This man refused to recant his writings at the Diet of Worms.
question.text: Name this German theologian, who, angered by the Catholic Church's use of indulgences, launched the Protestant Reformation by publishing his Ninety-FIve Theses.
question.clue: This man declared "here I stand, I can do other" before he was excommunicated by the bull Exsurge Domine , which was issued by Pope Leo X after the Diet of Worms .

swap.leadin: This leader was nicknamed the "Iron Chancellor" for conducting diplomacy using the strategy of Realpolitik.
swap.text: Name this Prussian statesman, who masterminded the Unification of Germany.
swap.clue: This man modified Count Benedetti's words in the doctored Ems Dispatch to instigate a war between his country and France.

question.leadin: Name these things associated with the unification of Germany.
question.text: Germany had been unified after various German lands had come together to defeat France in this war in 1870.
question.clue: During this war, Marshal Bazaine retreated his Army of the Rhine from the battle of Gravelotte to the town of Metz.

swap.leadin: Answer these questions about Beer Hall Putsch.
swap.text: The Beer Hall Putsch happened in this city. This capital of Bavaria was also the site of the 1972 Summer Olympics, where 12 Israeli athletes were murdered.
swap.clue: That used in Rollerball is the BMW Headquarters and Museum.

question.leadin: The father of this man forced him to watch the execution of his friend after trying to escape the royal court.
question.text: Identify this enlightened despot who fought the 7 Year's War against Austria.
question.clue: This ruler preemptively invaded Saxony to start a war in which his country was saved by the Miracle of the House of Brandenburg.

swap.leadin: The Guillaume ["Ghee-YOAM"] Affair forced the resignation of a chancellor of this country after it was revealed one of his aides was a spy.
swap.text: Name this no-longer existing country, which reunited with its eastern neighbor in 1990. The Stasi infiltrated the office of Willy Brandt, a chancellor of this country.
swap.answerHtml: West Germany [or Federal Republic of Germany; prompt on Germany; do NOT accept “East Germany” or “German Democratic Republic”]
swap.clue: This nation gained the Saarland in 1957, and it had a capital at Bonn.

question.leadin: As a result of this event, Hermann Goring committed suicide.
question.text: Name this set of tribunals, held in a namesake Bavarian city, during which Rudolf Hess and other leaders of a defeated government were prosecuted for crimes against humanity.
question.clue: Robert Ley committed suicide before the conclusion of this event, which was held at the Palace of Justice.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Nazi assassination plots.
swap.text: This commander committed suicide after being implicated in Claus von Stauffenberg's 20th of July Plot. This "desert fox" commanded the victorious forces at the Battle of Kasserine Pass.
swap.clue: This man was allowed to commit suicide, rather than face trial, after being implicated in Claus von Stauffenberg's ("klaus von stow-fehn-behrg's") July 20th plot.

question.text: This group gifted gyrfalcons to kings and popes after training them in Marienburg Castle. Vytautas the Great defeated this group at the 1410 Battle of Grunwald.
question.clue: The Golden Bull of Rimini confirmed some land holdings of this group, which absorbed the Livonian Order.

swap.text: The Spartacists sought to establish a Soviet-style state in the place of this post World War I German government, which held power until the establishment of the Third Reich.
swap.clue: The Spartacist League disbanded shortly after this government executed its leaders Walter Liebknecht and Rosa Luxemburg.

question.text: During this event of November 9, 1923, Hitler and Ludendorff attempted to take control of Munich.
question.clue: Its leader started it with the proclamation that "The National Revolution has begun" and this event ended after a brief firefight between insurgents and police in the Residenzstrasse.

swap.leadin: This conservative signed the Enabling act of 1933, officially handing power to Hitler.
swap.text: Name this German Field Marshal who was the namesake of a zeppelin that crashed in 1937.
swap.clue: This man was reviled by Hitler, who referred to him as "that old fool" and "that old reactionary" during his time as president of the Weimar ] Republic.

question.leadin: In 1956, a French protectorate in this region joined West Germany under the Treaty of Luxembourg.
question.text: Identify this coal-rich state in western Germany. A territory in this region was earlier joined to Germany after a 1935 plebiscite.
question.answerHtml: Saarland [accept Saar Protectorate or Territory of the Saar Basin]
question.clue: The Treaty of Versailles made this area an autonmous territory and gave France its coal fields. In a 1935 plebiscite, ninety percent of its voters favored reunion with Germany.

swap.text: Germany prescribed Pervitin en masse to its troops during an invasion of this region. This Czech region was annexed by Germany prior to World War II.
swap.clue: Chamberlain agreed to concede the occupation of this German-speaking region to appease Hitler.

question.text: In addition to destroying Hirschfeld's institute, Nazi Germany imprisoned gay men in concentration camps, where this symbol was used to identify them. Lesbians and trans men were assigned a black variant of this symbol as "asocials".
question.answerHtml: pink triangle [accept rosa Dreieck, prompt on partial answer]
question.clue: Three of these symbols appear in the corners of an Amsterdam monument commemorating LGBTQ+ victims of the Nazi regime. This symbol also appears above the words SILENCE=DEATH in an AIDS crisis-era poster.

swap.leadin: Most paperback editions of this book preface it with a "Memoir" by Gerhard Leibholz, which relates that the author was executed by the Nazis at Flossenburg.
swap.text: Name this work of Christian theology. It implores its readers to reject "cheap grace," which it defines as "the grace we bestow upon ourselves."

question.leadin: Albert the Bear was an oft-friend and an oft-rival of this Duke of Saxony.
question.text: Name this member of the House of Welf, a cousin of Frederick Barbarossa who developed the cities of Munich and Lubeck. His nickname also references an animal.
question.answerHtml: Henry the Lion [or Henry III; or Henry XII; prompt on “Henry”]
question.clue: This man commissioned a monk named Herimann to illustrate a 41-page gospel that sold for over $7 million in 1983.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about airlifts in American history.
swap.text: To counter a Soviet blockade in 1948, the American and British air forces coordinated this massive airlift that transported over two million tons of coal and food.
swap.clue: Commanded by William Tunner, it consisted of components known as "Easy" and "Willie," and it was also coordinated by Curtis LeMay.

question.leadin: Their 1819 passage was sparked by the murder of August von Kotzebue by a student.
question.text: Name these series of laws that placed government agents in all universities, put all newspapers under government supervision, and expelled overly liberal teachers and students.
question.clue: Burschenschaften fraternities were banned by these laws, which created an investigatory committee in Mainz to investigate "revolutionary activities" in the German states and gave the Diet censorship powers.

swap.text: The Herero Genocide was largely the handiwork of this German commander, who drove the Herero into the desert after the Battle of Waterberg, poisoned their water, and encircled the desert with his soldiers so that they could not escape.
swap.clue: This German commander wiped out the Hereros as commander in chief of German South West Africa, by cornering them into the Kalahari Desert, and poisoning their water Kefka-style.
